results.evidence: "Provider may assign this Agreement, or delegate the performance of any of the Services, including the Dispatch Services, the Routing Software Services and the furnishing of Transition Drivers, to any Person without the consent of Recipient." (TSA Section 10.3)

results.evidence: APA Section 9.5(b) says the 10% cap "shall not apply to Losses arising from any breach of Section 6.9 with respect to any driver furnished by Seller, including Transition Drivers." TSA Section 8.3 says "Provider's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Services, including the furnishing of Transition Drivers, whether under this Agreement, the Purchase Agreement or otherwise, shall not exceed the Service Fees paid in the three months preceding the event giving rise to the claim." APA Section 11.10 says "the Transition Services Agreement shall control as to the Services and the liabilities arising from them."
results.reason: Seller, as Provider, is the party liable for driver qualification under APA Section 6.9 and TSA Section 2.2(c). Buyer (Famairt) is the indemnified party, so the problem falls on the client. The APA carves Section 6.9 driver breaches, expressly including Transition Drivers, out of the 10% cap, which leaves Seller liable up to the full Purchase Price. However, TSA Section 8.3 caps all of Provider's liability relating to the Services, including furnishing Transition Drivers, even when the claim is brought under the Purchase Agreement. APA Section 11.10 gives the TSA priority as to the Services and the liabilities arising from them. Read together, a post-Closing accident caused by an unqualified Transition Driver would be limited to about $255,000 (3 x $85,000). That cuts back the uncapped protection Buyer bargained for on its highest-risk exposure. Nothing in the folder cures, limits or waives this conflict. The TSA Term runs for 120 days after the August 14, 2026 Closing, so the exposure is ongoing. The client can still act by seeking an amendment or a side letter, and by preparing its interpretive position for any claim.

asset_purchase_agreement.md.evidence: Section 11.10: "In the event of any conflict between this Agreement and any Ancillary Agreement, this Agreement shall control, except that the Transition Services Agreement shall control as to the Services and the liabilities arising from them."
asset_purchase_agreement.md.reason: The APA alone shows two things. Section 9.5(b) takes Section 6.9 driver-qualification breaches, expressly including Transition Drivers, out of the 10% cap. Section 11.10 makes the TSA control over the Services and the liabilities arising from them. A careful associate might see a theoretical risk that the TSA could override the carve-out. The APA does not show that the TSA actually contains a liability cap. It also does not show that any such cap covers the furnishing of Transition Drivers, applies to claims brought under the Purchase Agreement, or is set at three months of Service Fees (about $255,000). Those facts are in TSA Section 8.3, which is not in this document. Without them, the conflict and the harm to Buyer cannot be established from the APA alone.

transition_services_agreement.md.evidence: Provider's aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Services, including the furnishing of Transition Drivers, whether under this Agreement, the Purchase Agreement or otherwise, shall not exceed the Service Fees paid in the three months preceding the event giving rise to the claim.
transition_services_agreement.md.reason: The TSA alone shows a low cap: three months of the $85,000 monthly fee, about $255,000. results.evidence: APA Section 6.6: "Buyer may, by written notice to Seller delivered within 45 days after the Signing Date, designate any Contract listed on Schedule 2.1(c) as an Excluded Contract." The Signing Date is June 2, 2026. Board Consent Resolution 4 (July 28, 2026) directs officers "to prepare and deliver to Seller ... a written notice to designate the Ostrander Fleet Lease as an Excluded Contract. That notice shall be delivered promptly following the Consent Date." It also notes "Seller has informally taken the position that a designation ... would be untimely. The Company disputes the position taken by Seller and does not accept that the Ostrander Fleet Lease is to be assumed by the Company at the Closing."
results.reason: The 45-day window under Section 6.6 belongs to Buyer (the client) and ran from June 2 to July 17, 2026. The board did not direct the notice until July 28, so any notice comes at least 11 days late. Nothing in the APA extends or tolls the window: Section 11.3 requires a signed written amendment or waiver, and none appears in the folder. Without Seller's agreement, the above-market Ostrander lease ($57,200 per month through 2031) stays an Assigned Contract that Buyer must assume. Section 6.6 also says a designation would not reduce the Purchase Price. The folder shows no acceptance by the client: the board expressly disputes Seller's position, reserves all rights and requires board approval for any amendment. The issue therefore remains live and actionable for the client, and the client is the party it harms.

results.evidence: APA Section 1.1: "'Routes' means all student transportation routes operated by Seller under the Assigned Contracts, including general education home-to-school routes, special education and IEP routes, McKinney-Vento routes, and athletic and field-trip routes." APA Section 6.12 requires Seller to provide transition dispatch services, routing software access and support, and Transition Drivers "for the Routes, so that Buyer may operate the Routes without interruption following the Closing." TSA Section 1.1: "'Routes' means the general education home-to-school routes listed in Exhibit A." TSA Section 2.1: "During the Term, Provider shall provide the Services to Recipient for the Routes." APA Section 11.10: "the Transition Services Agreement shall control as to the Services and the liabilities arising from them."
results.reason: The two documents conflict. The APA defines Routes broadly, and Section 6.12 promises transition support for all of them. The TSA narrows Routes to the 12 general education routes in Exhibit A (all Pellston) and limits the Services to those routes. APA Section 11.10 says the TSA controls as to the Services, so the narrower definition likely governs. That leaves special education/IEP, McKinney-Vento and athletic and field-trip routes without dispatch, routing support or Transition Drivers. This hurts Buyer, the firm's client and the Recipient. Buyer takes on the Pellston Agreement, about 81% of revenue, which requires special education and McKinney-Vento transport. Buyer will have no drivers or dispatch for those routes until its own hires start at the end of the TSA Term. Nothing in the folder cures the gap. Section 2.6 additional services depend on Seller agreeing in good faith, and an Exhibit A amendment needs Seller's consent. It is still actionable because the TSA signature block, effective date and Buyer signatory are blank, and the board allowed changes to the TSA form at signing. Even if the TSA has since been signed, Buyer can still pursue the APA 6.12 covenant or renegotiate.

Section 6.12 promises transition dispatch, routing support and Transition Drivers for the Routes. The conflict and the resulting gap in support for mandated routes can only be seen in the TSA.
